Experiments that changed questions

The Barnum effect: one horoscope for everyone

A lecturer gave his students the "same" personality profile. Almost all found it very accurate.

In 1948, the psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students a personality test and a week later handed each one a supposedly personal report. He asked them to rate its accuracy from 0 to 5. The average was 4.26. Everyone had received the same text, partly taken from an astrology book.

Sentences that fit anyone

The text said things like "You have a great need for other people to like and admire you" or "At times you are extroverted and sociable, while at other times you are introverted and reserved". They are vague, mostly flattering statements that almost anyone recognises as their own.

It is called the Barnum effect, after the circus showman P. T. Barnum, credited with the phrase "we've got something for everyone". It explains the success of horoscopes, palm reading and some online tests. That is why a good psychological instrument must show that it distinguishes between people.

References

  1. Forer, B. R. (1949). The fallacy of personal validation. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 44(1), 118–123.
